turns.doctor_question: Hello, welcome. What brings you into the clinic today?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, yeah, thanks. Um, well, I guess the main thing is that I just... I get pulled off track by every little sound or thought. It's getting really frustrating, to be honest. 

Like, just as an example, the other day I was sitting down trying to work on a job application—because I've been trying to find something, you know, and it's tough out there—so I'm sitting at my laptop, and I'm telling myself to just focus on this one form. But then a car drives by outside. Not even a loud car, just a regular car going down the street, and I'm immediately looking out the window to see what it is. Or my phone screen will light up out of the corner of my eye, and even if it's just spam, I grab it. Or I'll just get some totally random idea in my head, like... I don't know, suddenly wondering what happened to this guy I knew in high school, or remembering a video I meant to watch. 

And before I even notice it, that random idea or that little noise just sends me somewhere else entirely. I'll be in a totally different room doing something completely different, or I'll be three pages deep on the internet, before I realize I completely abandoned the application. It just happens all the time, with everything I try to do, and I just can't seem to stop it.

symptom_reasoning.S002: The patient describes being unable to maintain focus on tasks like job applications, stating they abandon tasks and this happens 'all the time, with everything I try to do'.
symptom_reasoning.S008: The patient explicitly states they are easily pulled off track by extraneous stimuli (a car outside, a phone screen) and unrelated thoughts (random ideas, remembering a video).

turns.doctor_question: Did you experience similar difficulties with attention and distractibility when you were a child?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, oh man, absolutely. I mean, it goes way, way back. Like, I remember being in, what was it, maybe second or third grade? Elementary school, for sure. My mom used to get so frustrated because every single parent-teacher conference was the exact same conversation. The teachers were always, and I mean always, moving my seat. First I'd be in the back, then I'd be up front right next to the teacher's desk, then I'd be isolated in a corner because I just couldn't stop talking to whoever was next to me. I would just blurt things out, you know? Like, the teacher would be in the middle of a sentence explaining math or something, and a thought would pop into my head, and I'd just say it out loud without even realizing I was interrupting. 

And the homework... oh, don't even get me started on the homework. I'd do it sometimes, sure, but then I'd leave it on the kitchen table, or it would get crumpled up at the bottom of my backpack under a bunch of old permission slips and candy wrappers, and I'd completely forget to turn it in. Or when we had those worksheets in class, I would just blast right through them. I'd want to be the first one done, or I just wanted to go to recess, so I'd fill it out as fast as humanly possible. And then I'd get it back covered in red ink because I didn't read the instructions right, or I skipped half the questions, or I added instead of subtracted... just, like, really dumb, careless mistakes that I wouldn't have made if I had just slowed down for two seconds. But I just couldn't slow down. It was like I had one speed, and it was just... go. So yeah, it's definitely been happening since I was a little kid. It's just always been like this.

symptom_reasoning.S001: Patient describes making careless mistakes on worksheets, like adding instead of subtracting and skipping questions.
symptom_reasoning.S004: Patient mentions not reading instructions correctly and failing to properly complete and turn in schoolwork.
symptom_reasoning.S005: Patient describes a disorganized backpack filled with crumpled homework, old permission slips, and candy wrappers.
symptom_reasoning.S009: Patient notes completely forgetting to turn in their homework.
symptom_reasoning.S014: Patient describes themselves as having 'one speed, and it was just... go', indicating constant activity.
symptom_reasoning.S015: Patient states they 'couldn't stop talking' to classmates, leading to their seat being moved frequently.
symptom_reasoning.S016: Patient recalls blurting things out while the teacher was in the middle of a sentence.
symptom_reasoning.S018: Patient explicitly mentions interrupting the teacher by speaking out loud mid-sentence.

turns.doctor_question: Nowadays, do you find yourself feeling physically restless, fidgety, or having a hard time sitting still?
turns.patient_response:
Yeah, definitely. I mean, it's almost like I have this nervous energy that just has to go somewhere, you know? Like, if I'm sitting down talking to someone—whether it's hanging out with a friend, or even just sitting here right now—my leg is usually bouncing up and down. It's like a reflex at this point. I don't even notice I'm doing it until someone points it out or puts their hand on my knee to get me to stop. 

And if it's not my leg, it's my hands. I always have to have something in my hands. If there's a pen on the table, I'm clicking it over and over, or I'm taking the cap off and putting it back on, or I'm flipping it around my fingers. Or my keys! I'll just reach into my pocket and start jingling my keys or tracing the jagged edges of them with my thumb. It's like my body just refuses to be completely still. Even when I'm watching TV at home and I'm supposed to be relaxing, I'm shifting around on the couch, flipping the remote over and over, or picking at the hem of my shirt. It's just... constant. I honestly can't remember the last time I just sat perfectly still without some part of me moving or messing with something. It's like my brain is moving too fast and my body is just trying to keep up with it, even if I'm just sitting in a chair.

symptom_reasoning.S010: The patient explicitly describes bouncing their leg, clicking pens, jingling keys, and shifting around on the couch.
symptom_reasoning.S012: The patient describes having a 'nervous energy' and states that their body 'refuses to be completely still,' indicating a strong feeling of physical restlessness.
